result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.minimum_spanning_tree()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the minimum spanning tree using Kruskal's algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L45751-L45883){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.minimum_spanning_tree( weight_attr=None, return_subgraph=True, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Minimum spanning tree](/assets/graphs/minimum-spanning-tree.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node weighted graph with edge weights 1 to 7. The minimum spanning tree edges A–C (1), B–D (2), C–D (3), and B–E (6) are in the accent color and connect every node; the other edges are faded. The card lists the four tree edges and their total weight, 1 + 2 + 3 + 6 = 12." width="100%"} A minimum spanning tree (MST) is a subset of edges that connects all nodes with the minimum total edge weight, without forming any cycle. For a connected graph with `n` nodes it has exactly `n - 1` edges. Kruskal's algorithm sorts the edges from lightest to heaviest and keeps each edge that joins two not-yet-connected parts of the tree, using a union-find structure for efficient cycle detection. Minimum spanning trees are used for: - designing the cheapest network (cables, pipes, roads) that still reaches every site - extracting a sparse "skeleton" of a dense similarity or distance network - single-linkage clustering (cut the heaviest MST edges to split the data into groups) - approximation algorithms, such as for the traveling salesperson problem Edge direction is ignored, so on a directed graph the result is a spanning tree of the underlying undirected graph (the chosen edges keep their original orientation). If the graph is disconnected, the result is a minimum spanning *forest*: one tree per connected component. Self-loops are never selected, and among parallel edges only the lightest can be chosen. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute to use as the weight. If `None` (the default), each edge's weight field is used (edges on an unweighted graph count as `1.0`, so any spanning tree is minimal). If a name is given, edges that lack the attribute, or hold a non-numeric value, are treated as weight `1.0`. [return_subgraph]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (the default), returns a new `Graph` containing every node of the original graph and only the tree edges. If `False`, returns the IDs of the selected edges (as strings) in the order Kruskal's algorithm picked them, from lightest to heaviest; this is cheaper when you only need to know which edges belong to the tree. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph or list[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_subgraph=` is `True`: a new `Graph` with the same directedness and weighting, every node of the original (same IDs, labels and attributes) and the tree edges (same IDs, weights and attributes). If `return_subgraph=` is `False`: a list of edge ID strings referring to edges of the original graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Kruskal's algorithm sorts the $|E|$ edges by weight in $O(E \log E)$ and admits each into the growing forest whenever its endpoints belong to different components, checked with a union-find structure whose near-constant amortized cost per query keeps the sort as the dominant term. On a disconnected graph the result is a *spanning forest*, one MST per component, rather than a single tree. The sort is stable, so ties among equal-weight edges are broken by the order in which the edges are stored (normally the order they were added), and the returned tree is deterministic even when several MSTs share the minimum weight. ## Examples {.doc-examples} This 4-cycle plus one diagonal has 5 edges total, but connecting all 4 nodes only requires 3 of them -- the MST keeps the 3 cheapest edges that avoid forming a cycle: ::: {#b37a0fbe .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True) g.add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges( [("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 2.0), ("C", "D", 3.0), ("D", "A", 4.0), ("A", "C", 5.0)] ) mst = g.minimum_spanning_tree() # Returns 3 (connects all 4 nodes with the minimum number of edges) mst.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: Summing the weights of the tree's edges gives the total cost of the cheapest network that connects every node: ::: {#fed2261f .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Returns 6.0 (edges A-B, B-C, C-D, skipping the two priciest edges) sum(mst.get_edge(eid).weight for eid in mst.get_edge_ids()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 6.0 ``` ::: ::: With `return_subgraph=False`, the result is a list of edge IDs from the original graph, ordered from lightest to heaviest. Looking those edges up in `g` shows which connections were kept: ::: {#e1dbb85a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} edge_ids = g.minimum_spanning_tree(return_subgraph=False) [ (g.get_label_from_id(e.source), g.get_label_from_id(e.target), e.weight) for e in (g.get_edge(int(eid)) for eid in edge_ids) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [('A', 'B', 1.0), ('B', 'C', 2.0), ('C', 'D', 3.0)] ``` ::: ::: Use `weight_attr=` to build the tree from a different edge attribute. Here the edges carry a `length`, and the tree favors the shortest connections instead of the lowest `weight`: ::: {#ab229448 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} roads = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B", {"length": 4.0}), ("B", "C", {"length": 1.0}), ("A", "C", {"length": 2.0}), ] ) ) ids = roads.minimum_spanning_tree(weight_attr="length", return_subgraph=False) [ (roads.get_label_from_id(e.source), roads.get_label_from_id(e.target)) for e in (roads.get_edge(int(eid)) for eid in ids) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [('B', 'C'), ('A', 'C')] ``` ::: :::
